title: JWT helper functions
idea: A JWT helper module is one file, `src/utils/jwt.js`, that holds every call to `jsonwebtoken`. Everything else calls `signToken` or `verifyToken`.
points: `signToken(user)` builds the claims `{ sub, email }` and signs them for one hour.
`verifyToken(token)` returns the claims, or throws if the token is bad or expired.
A thrown error lets the caller choose the response. The helper never touches `res`.
Login still returns `200 { token }`. Only the signing code moved.

hero.title: Same behaviour, one place to change it

left.title: Without helpers
items: Login calls `jwt.sign` with its own options
The middleware would call `jwt.verify` the same way
One call can forget to restrict `algorithms`

right.title: With one helper file
items: Both helpers read `JWT_SECRET` and allow only HS256
Callers import two names and nothing else
A new rule is a one-file edit

hero.verdict: Callers say what they want. `jwt.js` decides how.

code.title: src/utils/jwt.js
code.caption: The two helpers are the new file. The lines under the setup comment try them out.

walk.text: `signToken` sets the claims and the options. `sub` is a string; the lifetime is one hour.
`verifyToken` accepts only HS256, the signing method, so any other kind is refused.
Both read `JWT_SECRET` when called. No other file needs to know it.
Sign a token for Ada, verify it, and print the claims and the lifetime in seconds.
Three bad tokens: wrong secret, expired, junk. Each one throws; the caller decides what that means.

code.title: Login controller, after
code.caption: The login controller shrinks. The route, the request and the response do not change.

pitfalls: Import `jsonwebtoken` only in `jwt.js`. A stray `jwt.verify` elsewhere can skip the checks.
Let `verifyToken` throw. Catching inside it hides failures from the middleware.
Keep `JWT_SECRET` in the environment, not in `jwt.js`. If it is unset, both helpers throw.

quiz.why: `signToken` stores `String(user.id)`. The `sub` claim comes back as the string `'7'`, and `typeof` reports it.

takeaway: One file owns every `jsonwebtoken` call; everything else uses two functions.

starters: Should the secret be read once at startup or on every call?
How would I test `signToken` and `verifyToken` on their own?
